title: Χελιδὼν καὶ δράκων
part: The Swallow and the Snake (Chambry 347 · Perry 227)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 347 (= Perry 227). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Χελιδὼν ἔν τινι δικαστηρίῳ νεοττοποιησαμένη ἐξέπτη· δράκων δὲ προσερπύσας κατέφαγεν αὐτῆς τοὺς νεοττούς.
sentences.tr: Chelidōn en tini dikastēriōi neottopoiēsamenē exeptē· drakōn de proserpysas katephagen autēs tous neottous.
sentences.l: A swallow, having made her nest in a certain law-court, flew out; and a snake, having crept up, devoured her nestlings.
sentences.i: A swallow had made her nest in one of the law-courts and flew out; and a snake crept up and devoured her nestlings.
sentences.n: δικαστήριον is the court where suits are heard — set down in the first line because the whole fable turns on it. νεοττοποιέομαι is middle, to make a nest for oneself, and it is built from the same νεοττοί, nestlings, that are eaten at the end of the line. προσερπύσας is the aorist participle of ἑρπύζω, 'creep', not of ἕρπω.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ἐπανελθοῦσα καὶ τὴν καλιὰν κενὴν εὑροῦσα ὑπερπαθῶς ἔστενεν.
sentences.tr: Hē de epanelthousa kai tēn kalian kenēn heurousa hyperpathōs estenen.
sentences.l: And she, having come back and having found the nest empty, groaned beyond measure.
sentences.i: When she came back and found the nest empty, she fell to groaning in an agony of grief.
sentences.n: Two aorist participles for what is over, then the imperfect ἔστενεν for the groaning that goes on. κενήν is predicative with εὑροῦσα: she found the nest empty, rather than finding an empty nest.

sentences.t: Ἑτέρας δὲ χελιδόνος παρηγορεῖν αὐτὴν πειρωμένης καὶ λεγούσης ⟨ὅτι⟩ οὐ μόνον αὐτὴν τέκνα ἀποβαλεῖν συμβέβηκεν, ὑποτυχοῦσα εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε οὐ τοσοῦτον ἐπὶ τοῖς τέκνοις κλαίω ὅσον ὅτι ἐν τούτῳ τῷ τόπῳ ἠδίκημαι ἐν ᾧ οἱ ἀδικούμενοι βοηθείας τυγχάνουσιν. »
sentences.tr: Heteras de chelidonos parēgorein autēn peirōmenēs kai legousēs ⟨hoti⟩ ou monon autēn tekna apobalein symbebēken, hypotychousa eipen· « All’ egōge ou tosouton epi tois teknois klaiō hoson hoti en toutōi tōi topōi ēdikēmai en hōi hoi adikoumenoi boētheias tynchanousin. »
sentences.l: And another swallow trying to comfort her and saying ⟨that⟩ it has not befallen her alone to lose children, she, taking-up-the-word, said: « But I for my part weep not so much over the children as because in this place I have been wronged, in which those who are wronged obtain help. »
sentences.i: Another swallow tried to comfort her, saying that she was not the only one to whom the loss of children had come; but she took up the word and said: « It is not so much for my children that I weep as that I have been wronged in the very place where the wronged find help. »
sentences.n: A genitive absolute (Ἑτέρας … πειρωμένης καὶ λεγούσης) holds the other swallow's speech open while the answer comes — the fable's usual way of running two actions at once. ⟨ὅτι⟩ is Chambry's own supplement, the angle brackets marking a word he adds to introduce the reported clause. ὑποτυχοῦσα is the house 'taking-up-the-word': a reply, never a seizing. οὐ τοσοῦτον … ὅσον ὅτι is 'not so much … as that'. ἠδίκημαι is perfect — the wrong is done and stands.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι πολλάκις χαλεπώτεραι γίνονται τοῖς πάσχουσιν αἱ συμφοραί, ὅταν ὑφ’ ὧν ἥκιστα προσεδόκησαν ὑφίστωνται.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti pollakis chalepōterai ginontai tois paschousin hai symphorai, hotan hyph’ hōn hēkista prosedokēsan hyphistōntai.
sentences.l: The story shows that often misfortunes become harder for those who suffer them, when they undergo them at the hands of those from whom they least expected them.
sentences.n: ὑφ’ ὧν is ὑπό with the relative, marking the agent: the harm comes from the very quarter that was trusted. ὅταν with the subjunctive ὑφίστωνται makes the case a general one, whenever it arises. The subject of that verb is most easily the sufferers, though it can be read of the misfortunes themselves; the comparative χαλεπώτεραι names no 'than' — harder than they would otherwise have been.
